BQTLemma

GeometryTrianglesArea
Game: Drag the points to change a shape made of two pairs of parallel lines, and watch three triangle areas.
How to play: Drag A, B, C, D or E with a mouse or finger, or focus a point and use the arrow keys. Press Check the claim to compare the areas.
Look for the math

Bui Quang Tuan found a small surprise: move the points however you like, keeping two pairs of lines parallel, and one triangle always has half the combined area of two others. The original cut-the-knot article shows the same lemma with a GeoGebra drawing; this page uses the rules of the older Java applet.

Two pairs of parallel lines

A, B and C are collinear: they sit on one straight line. D and E are on the same side of it, with AD ∥ BE and BD ∥ CE. Moving D rebuilds E from those two rules; moving E rebuilds D. Drag any point and the shape follows.

Equal areas in a trapezoid

ABED is a trapezoid because AD and BE are parallel. Triangles ABD and AED share the base AD and reach the same parallel line, so their areas match: [ABD] = [AED]. The same argument in BCED gives [BCE] = [CDE]. Adding them, [ABD] + [BCE] = [AED] + [CDE].

The midpoint halves the distances

F is the midpoint of AC. Measure the perpendicular distances from A, F and C to the line DE: call them h_a, h_m and h_c. Because F is halfway along AC, h_m = (h_a + h_c)/2. Since [AED] = DE·h_a/2 and [CDE] = DE·h_c/2, their sum is DE·h_m = 2·[DEM]. So the lemma follows:

[DEM] = ([ABD] + [BCE]) / 2.

The logic test checks this on the starting picture and on 500 other layouts, using both the cross-product area and the applet's own Heron-formula area. When B is exactly at F, all three shaded triangles have the same area, as the article points out.

A product that stays put

The article adds a second fact. If h_b is the distance from B to DE, similar triangles give h_b/h_a = h_c/h_b, hence [ABD]·[BCE] = [BDE]². The logic test confirms that too on every layout it tries.

Try pulling B right next to F: the three shaded areas become equal, and the two numbers in the status line still agree.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
